newsitem.title: USA: Environmental group warns of new U.S. pipeline risks.
newsitem.headline: Environmental group warns of new U.S. pipeline risks.

text.p: Corporate cost-cutting, government cutbacks and ageing facilities have combined to threaten the trans-Alaska oil pipeline, an Alaska environmental group said in a study released Wednesday.
The report, "Pipeline in Peril," said the system's operator has failed to achieve promised repairs and reforms ordered by the federal government in 1993.

Alyeska Pipeline Service Co., operator of the 800-mile (1,300 km) pipeline and its Valdez marine terminal, continues to have safety problems that pose risks of fire, oil spills or explosions, said the 300-page report.
The report was issued by the Alaska Forum for Environmental Reponsibility, a Prince William Sound-based group established to monitor Alyeska's compliance with state and federal regulations.
"This is a landmark report," Alaska Forum President Stan Stephens, a charter boat operator in Valdez, said in a prepared statement.

"It shows that the integrity of the pipeline is questionable and that Alyeska is either unable or unwilling to address the root causes of the problem. Congress and the public need to heed the warnings of pipeline workers," Stephens said.
Report author Richard Fineberg said he used government documents and information from pipeline employees willing to act as confidential whistleblowers.
The report also faults federal and state regulators for oversight that the Alaska Forum believes is too lax.
Both Alyeska and government regulators defended their records.
"The first thing that I'd like to make perfectly clear (is) the pipeline is safe," Alyeska vice president Doug Webb told Anchorage television station KTUU.

A spokesman for the Joint Pipeline Office, the consortium of federal and state agencies that oversee Alyeska operations, said the company had made significant progress in addressing serious electrical and communications problems throughout the system.
"The pipeline, in our view, is not imperilled," Joint Pipeline Office spokesman Rob McWhorter told KTUU.

Alyeska, a consortium owned by seven oil companies with interests on Alaska's North Slope, was ordered to launch major reforms in 1993, when the U.S. Bureau of Land Management issued a critical audit of the system.
The company followed up with its own audit, which cited nearly 5,000 items that needed to be fixed.
The trans-Alaska pipeline delivers about 1.5 million barrels of oil daily.
